clue.text: Question upsetting Open University strange enough to hold a meeting (6)

indicators.note: to upset a thing is to turn it over, and in a down clue the letters turned over are read from the bottom up

blocks.note: q = question, as on an exam paper or in Q&A
the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university, is OU, stood on its head
rum is an old adjective for odd, as in 'a rum do'

explanation.surface: A question has rattled the Open University, which is strange enough to call everyone together.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM for strange is Victorian slang that survives mainly in crosswords, and the drink is the decoy. A down entry is the only place 'upsetting' can stand two letters on their heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present before a meeting can do any business.

clue.text: A couple of things holding up Starmer maybe announcing notable achievement? (4)

definitions.text: A couple of things holding up Starmer maybe
definitions.note: The definition describes the pair as one item, so it reads as a singular 'couple' where the answer is a plural.

indicators.note: to announce something is to say it out loud, so what is wanted is the word that sounds the same rather than the one spelt

blocks.note: a notable achievement is a feat, and the ear cannot tell it from the spelling the grid needs

explanation.surface: The two things propping up the Prime Minister are being announced as some sort of achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the British prime minister, and 'maybe' admits he is only one example of somebody standing on a pair. The homophone is exact, which is why the definition has to carry half the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Feet are what hold any standing person up, Starmer included — a definition by example, which is what 'maybe' is flagging.

clue.text: Engineer creates extremely significant four-dimensional object (9)

indicators.note: to engineer a thing is to contrive it into the shape you want, and letters can be contrived the same way
the extremes of a word are the letters at its two far ends, with nothing in between them

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
the outermost letters of Significant, its two extremes

explanation.surface: An engineer builds something of extreme significance.
explanation.walkthrough: A tesseract is the four-dimensional counterpart of the cube, made of eight cubes the way a cube is made of six squares. 'Extremely significant' reads as praise and asks for the ends of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tesseract is the four-dimensional analogue of a cube, the standard geometrical name for that shape.

clue.text: Case of gangs following party animals (4)

indicators.note: a case is what encloses a thing, so the letters wanted are the ones sitting on the outside
what follows something comes along after it, so these letters are written second

blocks.note: a do is a party, the British word for any bash from a wedding to office drinks
the outer letters of GangS

explanation.surface: A court case about gangs comes up straight after a crowd of party animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of' is the outside of a word rather than its contents, which catches anyone who hears 'case' as a container. 'Party animals' reads as one phrase and breaks in two, the second half being the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogs are animals, a definition by example so broad that it gives nothing at all away.

clue.text: Stone Age circles advanced over time (5)

indicators.note: to circle something is to go right round the outside of it, which is where this word ends up
in a down clue whatever is over something sits above it, so it is written first

blocks.note: the clue's own word, taken whole before it is opened up
a = advanced, as in an A-level
t = time, the letter physics gives it

explanation.surface: Stone Age circles grew more advanced as time went on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone Age' is the trap: the two words read as one era and only the first of them is the definition. A for advanced comes from the A-level, the exam English schools set at eighteen.
explanation.definitionFit: An agate is a banded semi-precious stone, the sort cut for cheap jewellery and for marbles.

clue.text: Rector interrupting two bishops? I can feel the chill (4)

definitions.note: The answer is an interjection, so the definition has to be the sentence a solver would say instead of making the noise.

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in part-way through, so this letter lands inside what was already there

blocks.note: a bishop is b on a chessboard and RR as the Right Reverend of his title, so two of them supply three letters
r = rector, the parish clergyman's title abbreviated on a church noticeboard

explanation.surface: A rector cuts across two bishops in conversation and the room turns cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The frosty silence after a rector talks over his bishops is the surface joke, and the chill is the answer's business too. Bishop lends crosswords both the chess letter and the Right Reverend of his style.
explanation.definitionFit: Brrr is the shiver written down, the noise a cold person makes and so the spoken way of saying you feel the chill.

clue.text: Diplomatic manoeuvre reached beginning of mutual arrangement (8)

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter and nothing after it
an arrangement is the order things have been put into, and this order is not the one the letters arrived in

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
the first letter of Mutual

explanation.surface: Two sides reached the start of a mutual arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: A demarche is the formal step one government takes towards another, usually a protest or an approach — worth owning, because the definition will not lead you there by guesswork. 'Mutual arrangement' hides the anagram word in plain diplomatic language.
explanation.definitionFit: Demarche is the borrowed French term for exactly that kind of move: a government's formal approach to another state.

clue.text: Amazing drug, crack? Something telling me to think twice (8)

definitions.text: Something telling me to think twice

blocks.note: super is the everyday word for amazing
e = ecstasy, the tablet the single letter stands for
a crack at something is a go at it, one attempt

explanation.surface: A dealer offers amazing drugs and crack, and something makes the buyer hesitate.
explanation.walkthrough: In Freud's model the superego is the conscience, the part that answers the id's first impulse, which is the voice the second half of the clue describes. 'Crack' is a drug on the surface and only an attempt underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: The superego is the moralising voice that checks impulse before it becomes action, so it is precisely what makes you think twice.

clue.text: Weed possibly represented danger (6)

indicators.note: one thing can be represented by another made of the very same parts, here the same six letters set out in a different order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A weed is being treated as a possible danger.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Weed' as a verb and the definition works. The noun senses — the plant, the cannabis, the feeble man — all lead nowhere, and only three of the clue's words are wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To garden is to work a plot, and weeding is the commonest of the jobs that counts as doing it — a verb defined by one of its parts.

clue.text: Inspired by preacher it established rituals (5)

indicators.note: to be inspired is literally to have something breathed into you, so the letters wanted are the ones breathed inside the words that follow

blocks.note: preacheR IT EStablished, five letters running straight across two word breaks

explanation.surface: Inspired by a preacher, a congregation set up ceremonies of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words live on the joins between words, and this one takes the end of one, the whole of the next and the start of a third. 'Inspired by' reads as admiration and means breathed into.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites are formal rituals: the set order of words and actions a ceremony has to follow.

clue.text: Nameless planet with rotation period of another, one of seven (8)

indicators.note: something nameless has had its name taken off it, and 'name' shortens to the single letter n

blocks.note: Saturn is the planet, and the n of name is what it gives up
a day is Earth's rotation period, Earth being the other planet

explanation.surface: A planet nobody names turns in the same time as another of seven such worlds.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven of the definition are days, though the clue spends its whole surface among planets. Losing 'name' as N is a convention worth owning, from the n. printed on a form.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturday is one of the week's seven days, a definition by example, and the only seven the clue will admit to.

clue.text: Hard to leave pet rodent with mother in city (9)

indicators.note: what leaves is no longer there, so the letter named ahead of it goes missing

blocks.note: a hamster is the pet rodent of the cage and wheel
h = hard, the grade stamped on a pencil, and the letter that goes
a dam is an animal's mother, the breeder's word for her

explanation.surface: Leaving a pet rodent with its mother in a city is a wrench.
explanation.walkthrough: Dam for mother comes from livestock breeding, where a foal's dam is its mother and its sire the father. The city ends with a real dam, the one on the Amstel it is named for.
explanation.definitionFit: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, so 'city' is a definition by example and hands over nothing.

clue.text: Lock for abandoned castle (5)

indicators.note: what has been abandoned is left behind, so those letters do not come along into the answer

blocks.note: a fortress is a castle, taken whole before it is cut
the clue's own 'for', the three letters dropped from the front

explanation.surface: A lock meant for a castle nobody lives in any more.
explanation.walkthrough: A tress is a lock of hair, not of a door, which is the sense the castle steers you away from. 'For' looks like a word about purpose and is really three letters to throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: A tress is a long lock of hair — the sense of 'lock' you brush rather than the one you turn a key in.

clue.text: Left before the end of having sex, needing straightening (5)

indicators.note: the end of a phrase is its very last letter, and this piece is slipped in just ahead of it

blocks.note: a couple at it are having sex, in the standard euphemism
l = left, as marked on a pair of gloves

explanation.surface: Somebody leaves before sex is over, and something is left needing straightening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At it' is the phrase the wordplay wants, and the insertion lands one letter short of its end. 'Left' looks like the past tense of leaving and gives up only the l of left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: Atilt means leaning out of true, which is exactly the state of anything that wants putting straight.

clue.text: Ban learner stuck in reverse (5)

indicators.note: something stuck in is wedged inside, so the letter goes between the others rather than beside them

blocks.note: to reverse a car is to back it
l = learner, the plate on a British learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A learner driver is stuck in reverse gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' looks like an instruction to turn letters round; it is a noun here, the gear. Unions used to black goods they refused to handle, which is where the definition comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To black something is to boycott it — the trade-union sense of refusing to handle goods, which amounts to banning them.

clue.text: See about - how should I put it - provider of relief (5)

blocks.note: lo is the old word for see or behold, as in 'lo and behold'
c = circa, the 'about' that goes before an uncertain date
um is the noise that fills the pause while you hunt for the right word

explanation.surface: A speaker gropes for the right word about someone who brings relief.
explanation.walkthrough: A locum is the stand-in a doctor's or vet's practice books while the regular one is away, so 'relief' means cover rather than comfort. The dashes are the setter hesitating out loud, and that hesitation is two of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum stands in for the regular doctor or clergyman, providing relief in the sense of cover for an absent colleague.

clue.text: Biomolecule? In DNA see variant with added oxygen (9)

indicators.note: a variant is the same material in another form, and letters in another form are letters in another order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
o = oxygen, its chemical symbol, thrown in with the other eight

explanation.surface: A look inside DNA turns up a variant carrying an extra oxygen atom.
explanation.walkthrough: Adenosine is adenine joined to a sugar, one of the units DNA and RNA are built from, so the surface describes the answer while hiding it. 'In DNA see' is three words of fodder pretending to be an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Adenosine is a biomolecule — definition by example, flagged by the question mark — the nucleoside that also carries energy round the cell as ATP.

clue.text: Care for vole as mate becomes tame (4)

indicators.note: the setter works an example instead of naming the device: mate and tame are the same four letters in a new order, and the next word is to be treated the same way

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A vole is cared for and grows tame, the way a mate does.
explanation.walkthrough: Very few clues demonstrate their own device, and this one spends five words doing it. The vole is the only thing in the clue that supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To love someone is to care for them, the plainest sense of the verb.

clue.text: Over in France nothing supported by talk promoter aligned with references (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue whatever supports something sits underneath it, so the supporting letters come last

blocks.note: o = over, the six balls a cricket scorebook records
rien is French for nothing
TED is the American organisation behind TED talks

explanation.surface: Over in France, nothing at all is being backed by a promoter of talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over in France' reads as one phrase and splits in two, the cricket over and then the French. TED has only been a crossword word for about fifteen years, but it is a talk promoter beyond argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Something oriented has been set in a known position relative to fixed reference points — the surveyor's and map-reader's sense of alignment.

clue.text: Church taking edge off unruly youngster (5)

indicators.note: the edge of a word is the letter standing at its rim, and taking it off leaves the rest behind

blocks.note: ch = church, as printed on an Ordnance Survey map
unruly is wild, and the w at its edge is what comes off

explanation.surface: The church is taking the edge off an unruly youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking edge off' does two jobs at once: it reads as calming the youngster down and it strips the first letter from the word for unruly. Ch for church is the map-maker's abbreviation rather than the hymn book's.
explanation.definitionFit: A child is a youngster, the plain synonym, and the unruly one of the surface is the same person.

clue.text: Munch cold cut (4)

blocks.note: c = cold, the letter on a British bathroom tap
to hew is to cut, the verb used of timber and stone

explanation.surface: Somebody munches a slice of cold cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold cut' is the whole trap: two words that read as a plate of sliced meat and break into a letter and a verb. To hew is to cut with an axe rather than a knife.
explanation.definitionFit: To chew is to munch: the same grinding of food between the teeth.

clue.text: Tree starts to sprout twigs before anything else (5)

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, and two words asked for their starts give a letter each

blocks.note: a fir is a tree, the one crosswords reach for when three letters are wanted
the opening letters of Sprout and Twigs

explanation.surface: A tree puts out twigs before it does anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: Most of the clue is definition: only three of its words supply letters, and 'starts to' looks like part of the tree's behaviour. The answer is an adverb here, not the front of a queue.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a thing first is to do it before anything else, the adverb in its ordinary sense of order.

clue.text: Recompense workers with time after they have lunch? (9)

indicators.note: what comes after something follows it, so these letters are written behind the earlier ones

blocks.note: lunch is taken at one o'clock, and 'at one' runs together into five letters
men are workers, as in the men on a building site
t = time, the letter physics gives it

explanation.surface: Workers are paid for their time once they have had lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Lunch at one is the joke, and the hour hides in the answer's first five letters. 'Workers' is usually ANTS in a crossword; here the plainer men are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Atonement is recompense in the sense of making up for a wrong, what you pay in apology rather than in wages.

clue.text: Tended to break asunder after the start (6)

indicators.note: to break a thing is to smash it into pieces that can be put back together in another order
the start is the first letter, so what comes after it is everything except that letter

blocks.note: aSUNDER without its opening a, six letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: Something tended to break apart shortly after it began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tended to break' is the trap — it reads as a tendency and is really the definition plus the anagram word. Dropping the a is the kind of trim 'after the start' always asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse someone is to tend them, looking after the sick, and the past tense matches the definition's.

clue.text: Impatient? Try one of the axes (5)

blocks.note: to try a thing is to test it, as a court tries a case
a graph labels its two axes x and y, so either letter answers to one of them

explanation.surface: An impatient person is invited to try one of the axes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axes' is the plural of two different words, and the pair wanted are the graph's, not the woodsman's. Try for test belongs as much to the courtroom as to the laboratory.
explanation.definitionFit: Testy means short-tempered and quick to bridle, the adjective for somebody with no patience to spare.

clue.text: Clear where the US put copper until late last year, reportedly (8)

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by mouth, so the sound of the words counts and their spelling does not

blocks.clueFragment: where the US put copper until late last year
blocks.note: America's one-cent coin was the copper penny, struck until the Mint stopped making it late in 2025, so copper went in a cent

explanation.surface: A report on where the United States kept its copper until the end of last year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is the metal here, not the policeman a British crossword usually means by it. The clue is dated by the news: the US Mint struck its last one-cent coin in 2025.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone innocent is in the clear, cleared of the charge rather than merely unlikely to have done it.

clue.text: Hope menu contents ready to serve customers (4)

indicators.note: the contents of a word are the letters shut inside it, with the ones at each end left out

blocks.note: the inside of hOPe, both ends dropped
the inside of mENu, both ends dropped

explanation.surface: You hope the menu on display means the place is ready for customers.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words give up their insides, two letters each, which is why 'contents' is plural. The hope and the menu make one restaurant picture and take two separate cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop or restaurant that is open is ready to serve customers — the word on the sign in the door.

clue.text: Age occasionally overlooked at film set (4)

indicators.note: letters overlooked on and off leave only every other one to be read

blocks.note: aT fIlM sEt, every second letter taken and the rest skipped

explanation.surface: On a film set they sometimes forget how old somebody is.
explanation.walkthrough: Alternate letters run straight through the gaps, so the last three words have to be read as one string of nine. The definition is the sense in 'the age of steam'.
explanation.definitionFit: An age and a time are both a named stretch of history — the age of steam, in Tudor times — so either noun does for the other.

clue.text: Boulder in the centre blocking rise of the sun (5)

indicators.note: the centre of a word is the one letter with the same number of letters on either side of it
something blocking a way sits in the middle of it, splitting what it interrupts in two

blocks.note: to soar is to rise
the middle letter of the seven in bouLder

explanation.surface: A boulder in the middle of the road is blocking the sunrise from view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise of the sun' reads as a sunrise and breaks in two, 'rise' being the word to translate and the last three words the definition. A seven-letter word has one letter dead centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar means of or belonging to the sun, as in solar power and solar eclipse.

clue.text: Hold out something that looks like a foot (4)

definitions.text: something that looks like a foot

blocks.note: to endure, to keep going until the end of something

blocks.clueFragment: something that looks like a foot
blocks.note: the cobbler's wooden mould, shaped like a foot, that a shoe is built around

explanation.surface: Somebody is asked to hold out a thing shaped like a foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together as one instruction, which is the whole difficulty. A shoemaker's version is the wooden foot the shoe is built around, and 'stick to your last' comes from it.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to hold out, to endure; and a last is the foot-shaped block a cobbler shapes a shoe on.

clue.text: Setter's announcement when article and part of speech censored (6)

indicators.note: what is censored is cut out and never printed, so those letters are struck from the word

blocks.note: the twelve-letter word that is about to lose two pieces
an is the indefinite article, and it goes from the front
noun is a part of speech, and its four letters follow straight on from the article

explanation.surface: The setter's announcement survives the censoring of an article and a part of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' in a crossword almost always means the compiler, so the temptation is to hunt for I or ME. The two censored pieces come out of the long word in the order the clue names them.
explanation.definitionFit: Cement is the stuff whose whole job is to set once it is mixed, so calling it a setter is a builder's joke rather than a dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Clergyman the first person to enter church (8)

indicators.note: to enter a building is to go inside it, so this letter goes within the word for one

blocks.note: a minster is a great church, as at York
i is the first-person pronoun, the word you use for yourself

explanation.surface: A clergyman is the first person through the church door.
explanation.walkthrough: A minster is a large church — York Minster, Westminster — and the first person is the grammarian's, not whoever arrived early. The container and the thing contained are both sitting in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister is a clergyman, the usual word for a Protestant or nonconformist pastor.
